shortlist.raw_text: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.

shortlist.raw_text: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

shortlist.raw_text: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

Article text (excerpt):
The Walmart Agent Gateway is now live with Muse support, with other apps and agents ‘on the way.’﻿
The Walmart Agent Gateway is now live with Muse support, with other apps and agents ‘on the way.’﻿
Walmart will now let Meta’s Muse shop on its website on your behalf, allowing the AI agent to find and purchase Black Friday deals. The retail giant is rolling out a live implementation of the Agent Gateway it announced last month , which helps AI agents find relevant products for you without sharing your purchase history, according to Walmart.
Muse can make purchases through Walmart’s “Agent Profiles,” which provide a dedicated space for agent activity within your Walmart customer account. These profiles also allow you to set spending limits, approve purchases, and check the purchase history of everything bought by Muse. While other online retailers like Amazon and eBay have blocked AI agents from browsing their platforms, Walmart says that support for Meta’s Muse is “just the beginning,” and that additional Walmart shopping experiences for other AI agents and apps are “on the way.”
Here are Walmart’s instructions for shopping its website via Muse:
1. Tell Muse what you need. For example, ask it to find a great TV deal or show you which Walmart Black Friday deals are available for delivery. Muse can help you explore products and build your basket.
2. Set your shopping rules. Muse will take you to Walmart to sign in, then bring you back to Muse. The first time you add an item to your cart, you’ll set up your Agent Profile on Walmart within your Walmart account, including a spending limit you’re comfortable with.
3. Check out. Complete your purchase within the conversation using a card saved in your Walmart account, with the same Walmart prices you’d find on Walmart.com. And if something isn’t quite right, Walmart’s return policy still applies.
This is the title for the native ad
text:
Most online retailers treat AI agents like web scrapers to be blocked.

Walmart is taking the opposite bet with Meta.

The retail giant rolled out a live implementation of its Agent Gateway, allowing Meta's Muse to find Black Friday deals and buy items directly on a user's behalf. Access is routed through dedicated Agent Profiles built into existing customer accounts.

Shoppers control the boundaries. Walmart allows account holders to set spending caps, approve individual purchases, and review transaction logs.

Checkout completes within the conversation using a saved card at standard Walmart.com prices. Walmart states the agent cannot see past purchase history, and standard return policies apply.

Amazon and eBay continue to block AI agents from browsing their platforms. Walmart claims integrating Muse is only the first step, with support for additional agents on the way.

Retailers will not stop AI shopping agents by blocking them. The advantage will go to platforms that offer controlled access to customer wallets.

Source: The Verge

#Retail #ArtificialIntelligence
alt_openings:
**Opening 1: Corrective**
Line 1: Retailers are not all fighting AI shopping agents.
Line 2: While Amazon and eBay block them, Walmart just opened its checkout system to Meta's Muse.
*When to prefer:* Use when writing for retail and e-commerce leaders who care about strategy shifts and market positioning.

**Opening 2: Tool as subject**
Line 1: Meta's Muse can now find and purchase Black Friday deals on Walmart.com.
Line 2: It buys products directly through your account using a system called Agent Gateway.
*When to prefer:* Use when the primary audience is product managers and tech professionals interested in functional AI deployment.

**Opening 3: Story in motion**
Line 1: Walmart just handed Meta's AI agent the keys to its checkout counter.
Line 2: You set a spending cap inside your account, and the bot handles the rest.
*When to prefer:* Use when aiming for maximum broad reach across non-technical managers who respond to clear narrative pictures.

Pick: The "Your X" opening from the main post ("Meta's AI agent can now log into Walmart and spend your money.") because it creates immediate personal stakes for the reader before explaining the technical mechanism behind it.
firewall_notes: "Meta's AI agent can now log into Walmart and spend your money." — Trips Rule 10 and 15: Gives away the hook before the fold and overstates agent autonomy beyond what the source supports.
"Instead of an AI bot surreptitiously scraping web pages, Meta's Muse operates inside dedicated Agent Profiles..." — Trips Rule 1: Uses the predictable "Instead of X, Y" machine framing.
The three bullet points under "Walmart built three specific controls..." — Trips Rule 3: Uses a triad list structure.
"Amazon and eBay are actively shutting out AI agents. Walmart is doing the exact opposite..." — Trips Rule 2: Parallel binary contrast that repeats previous context.
"Would you set a spending limit and let an AI handle your holiday shopping?" — Trips Rule 13: Standard AI engagement-bait closing question.
